prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
When you run git commit, the result is stored in a hidden directory called .git, and almost everything in there is built from just four kinds of thing: blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The first three live in a content-addressable object database under .git/objects, which is nothing more than a key-value store. Each object is compressed with zlib, and its key is the SHA hash of its contents, preceded by a short header giving the object's type and size. Because the name is derived from the content, two identical pieces of data always share a single object, and any change to the data produces a completely different name. That property is what makes Git history tamper-evident and cheap to store.

The simplest object is the blob, which holds the raw bytes of one file and nothing else. A blob has no filename, no permissions and no timestamp; it is just content. If you have ten copies of the same license file in different directories, Git stores one blob and refers to it ten times. If you rename a file without editing it, the blob is unchanged, which is partly why Git can detect renames so easily after the fact. You can see this for yourself by running git hash-object on a file and then git cat-file -p with the resulting hash, which prints the file back to you exactly as it was.

Names and permissions belong to the second kind of object, the tree. A tree represents one directory, and it is a list of entries, each pairing a mode, a name and the hash of something else. An entry that points to a blob is a file, and an entry that points to another tree is a subdirectory. The mode records whether a file is a regular file, an executable or a symbolic link. Because trees refer to other trees by hash, a whole project snapshot is described by a single root tree, and that one hash effectively summarizes every file and folder beneath it. If you change one line in a deeply nested file, you get a new blob for that file, a new tree for its directory, and new trees for every parent up to the root, while all the untouched siblings keep their old hashes and are shared with the previous snapshot. This is why Git stores snapshots rather than diffs and still stays compact.

The third kind of object is the commit, which is what you actually think of as a commit. It is a small text record containing the hash of the root tree, the hashes of zero or more parent commits, an author and a committer with timestamps, and finally the message you wrote. The root tree says what the project looked like, while the parent lines say where it came from. A normal commit has one parent, a merge commit has two or more, and the very first commit in a repository has none. Since each commit includes its parents' hashes, and those commits include theirs, the whole history forms a chain of hashes in which altering any old commit would change the hash of every commit after it. Running git cat-file -p HEAD will show you this record in plain text, and it is usually a surprisingly short thing to read.

Hashes are unfriendly to humans, so Git adds the fourth ingredient, refs, which are simply named pointers to commits. A ref is a tiny file under .git/refs whose entire content is a forty-character hash. Your local branches live in .git/refs/heads, so the file for main contains the hash of the latest commit on main. Tags live in .git/refs/tags, and the branches you track on a remote live in .git/refs/remotes. Creating a branch is therefore almost free, because Git only has to write one small file, and making a commit on a branch just means writing the new commit object and then updating that file to point at it. Nothing about the older commits changes at all.

One more file ties it all together, namely .git/HEAD, which records where you are currently working. Usually it holds a line such as ref: refs/heads/main, meaning that HEAD points at a branch, which in turn points at a commit. When you check out a specific commit instead of a branch, HEAD contains a raw hash, which is exactly the detached state that produces Git's well-known warning.

Putting this together, a commit is stored in a few steps. Git first writes a blob for each changed file, then writes trees from the bottom of your directory structure up to the root, then writes a commit object pointing at that root tree and at the previous commit, and finally moves the current branch ref forward. Over time Git packs many loose objects into compact packfiles and stores them as deltas against one another, but that is only a storage optimization, and the model of blobs, trees, commits and refs stays exactly the same.
